title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | 1100 | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: The Sicilian — Black plays the Accelerated Dragon, a fine choice at this level.
White plays the bishop to c4 — an Italian idea against the Sicilian, but it does not work the same way.
The reason: e6, blunting the bishop and preparing d5.
White pushes e5 — and here is a mind-blower: a very cool move becomes possible precisely because of the bishop on c4.
The move is d5 — associate the bishop on c4 with the possibility of d5. It plants a pawn in the centre.
If White takes the knight, Black takes the bishop, and a very interesting structure arises.
Doubled pawns, a ruined kingside — but look deeper.

It is hard for White to develop the bishop: if d3, Black takes, White recaptures, and the pawn on d3 becomes a sitting duck. Black has the two bishops, great in an open position, one already pre-developed to a fine square. And those 'weak' pawns are actually strong — they stop White controlling any share of the centre.
c5 is attacked — and b6 kills two birds: it defends the pawn and prepares to fianchetto the other bishop.

A lesson in flexibility: the natural bishop to a6, hitting the pawn, actually fails to the queen to a4, forking two undefended pieces. Be obsessed with undefended pieces — putting a piece on an undefended square should ring alarm bells.
So the bishop to b7 instead — then castle, and the knight to b4 can target that weak pawn.
White threatens a knight jump to d6 — but castling takes the sting out of it: even if the knight lands there, it is no longer a fork.

The knight to g5 looks scary, but it has no real threat. Black could play h6, but need not — go straight for the counter-attack. Taking on b2 would be bad, though — c5 and the queen to h5 — so keep the bishop for defence.

Find what is weak: the d3-pawn is White's biggest weakness, so target it with the knight to b4. If White tries the queen to h5, his position falls apart — Black takes on d3 with check, disarms the attack, and wins a piece.
The knight to d4 does not accomplish much — the knight to b4 is more purposeful. White is already in trouble.
First, annoy him — h6, get out of here — then take on d3. If the knight goes to f3, then the knight takes on d3 hits two pieces at once.
The knight takes on d3 — attacking the bishop, and now the knight on e4 has lost its pawn defender.
If White tries the bishop to d6 to save the piece, Black still takes the knight, ending up two pieces for a rook and a pawn — complete domination.

White is completely lost — the rook on b1 hangs, so Black can take either piece. Take with the bishop; but now White hits it back, so don't just defend — defend in a way that coordinates the most pieces. The queen to d5 is best, building a battery: threatening to wreck White's structure or force a queen trade, connecting the rooks. And it is not a real pin — the knight is not paralysed, so the knight takes on f4 counter-attacks the queen, and it is simply winning.

In review, the bishop to c4 is not amazing. The d5 idea shows up most famously in the Scotch Gambit — that Scotch-and-Italian mix — where after the knight to f6 and e5, d5 is the main theoretical continuation. Same concept here.

And those doubled pawns operate in tandem, partners in stopping White's centre — it is not easy for White to attack either. Try the queen to e2 to win one, and Black just counter-attacks and forces the queen back.
